title: Gecko: A Simulation Environment with Stateful Feedback for Refining Agent Tool Calls
claim: Adding our test-time refinement method consistently improves performance across many models and benchmarks compared with the same models without it.
layout: 1 circular radar chart split into 3 benchmark sectors, paired blue and red polylines
description: A single large circular radar chart divided into three sectors: BFCL v3 (top, light blue arc), τ²-retail (bottom left, orange) and τ²-airline (bottom right, green). Each sector has spokes labeled with LLM names such as GPT-4o, GPT-5-thinking, Gemini-3.0-pro, Deepseek-v3 and Qwen-3-14B. Two closed polylines run around the ring. A blue one is labeled 'w/o GATS' and a red one 'w/ GATS'. Numeric scores sit at each vertex, with blue values just inside and red values just outside. The red line lies outside the blue line on every spoke, so the gain is visible at a glance. The sector names sit in the empty center. A legend with two colored swatches is at the bottom. The eye goes first to the red outline hugging the outer ring.
caption: GATS uses Gecko’s feedback from simulated tool executions to iteratively refine tool calls, consistently improving the performance of different LLMs on BFCLv3 and τ2-bench.
abstract: The ability to use tools is fundamental for large language model (LLM) agents. Given a task, existing systems use LLMs to plan and generate tool calls, which are executed by real-world tools to complete the task. However, tool calls are prone to errors because they are generated primarily from the intrinsic capabilities of LLMs. Moreover, while it is useful to let LLMs iteratively refine the tool-call sequence using execution results from real tools, this process can be expensive and may cause unsafe side effects. To improve LLM tool calls and address issues caused by using real tools for refinement, we introduce Gecko, a stateful simulation environment that provides informative feedback for refining LLM tool calls before real execution. Specifically, Gecko combines rules and LLMs to check the validity of tool names and arguments, synthesize schema-conforming and state-consistent responses, and judge task completion against the user objective. These three types of feedback allow LLMs to refine their tool calls in simulation, forming a simple yet effective test-time scaling method named GATS. On BFCLv3 and $Ï^2$-bench, GATS consistently improves the performance of various LLMs.
